text: Course two covered UI Policies — rules that show, hide, require, or lock down a field on a table, reacting to another field on that same form, with no client script needed. A Catalog UI Policy does the identical conceptual job, but it operates on a variable on a catalog item's request form instead of a regular table field, and that distinction turns out to matter a great deal.

Catalog variables aren't stored as columns on a form's underlying table the way priority or assignment_group are — they live in item_option_new and sc_item_option, a fundamentally different structure. The standard UI Policy engine that watches table fields simply has no way to see or react to them, which is exactly why ServiceNow ships a separate object type, catalog_ui_policy, built specifically for variables.

A Catalog UI Policy carries the same three levers as its table-field counterpart. Visible shows or hides a variable based on a condition. Mandatory forces a requester to answer before submitting, but only when that condition is true. Read-only lets a requester see a value without being able to change it. Each policy runs entirely client-side, reacting live as the requester fills in the form.

Here's the worked example. A budget-increase catalog item has a Cost Center Override checkbox and a Manager Approval Reason text variable. The policy's condition checks whether Cost Center Override is true; its action makes Manager Approval Reason both visible and mandatory. For most requesters, who never touch the override, that reason field stays hidden and optional, keeping their form short and uncluttered.

A common early mistake is going looking for a newly built catalog variable inside the regular UI Policy list, or building a Catalog UI Policy and expecting it to control a real table field like short_description. Neither works, because the two object types watch entirely different kinds of data — knowing which one you actually need before building the condition saves real troubleshooting time.

Get the object type right, and the show-hide-mandatory logic just works, the same way it did for table fields back in course two. Next up: Record Producers, a type of catalog item that skips the standard request process entirely and writes straight to a different table.
